text: The Fabric of Everyday Life
Every Saturday at 6:30 a.m., long before the first customers
arrive, the vendors of the Riverbend Market begin unloading
their trucks. The market has operated on the same four-
block stretch of Alder Street since 1948, and by most
accounts it has never missed a week.
For now, the routine continues. By

Roughly 140 stalls now fill the street, up from 85 a decade
ago. According to the city's 2023 survey, the market draws
about 12,000 visitors on a typical weekend and generates
an estimated $4.2 million a year for the local economy (not
counting nearby cafes and shops).

sell is a reason to come downtown." Her best-selling item,
she added, is still the two-dollar bag of mixed greens.
The numbers support her. Foot traffic on market days is
38% higher than on other Saturdays, and three-quarters of
visitors told surveyors they also stopped somewhere else in
the neighborhood. Dr. Alan Whitfield, an economist at the
state university, calls this the "spillover effect."
Not everything is rosy. Stall fees rose from $35 to $50 per
day in January, and several long-time vendors say the
increase is hard to absorb. Parking remains the most
common complaint: the nearest public garage has only 220
spaces, and it is usually full by 9:15 a.m.
The city council is weighing a proposal to close two
additional blocks to cars between May 1 and October 31.
Supporters argue the change would add room for 40 more
stalls; opponents worry about deliveries and access for
older residents.
